'''William Henry Kruskal''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|r|ʌ|s|k|əl}}; October 10, 1919 – April 21, 2005) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[statistician]].  He is best known for having formulated the [[Kruskal–Wallis one-way analysis of variance]] (together with [[W. Allen Wallis]]), a widely used [[non-parametric statistics|nonparametric statistical method]].

==Biography==
Kruskal was born to a [[American Jews|Jewish]] family<ref>[http://americanjewisharchives.org/publications/journal/PDF/1972_24_01_00_brown.pdf American Jewish Archives: "Two Baltic Families Who Came to America The Jacobsons and the Kruskals, 1870-1970" by RICHARD D. BROWN] January 24, 1972</ref> in [[New York City]] to a successful fur wholesaler.<ref name="Obit">{{cite news|last1=Sheehan |first1=Charles |title=Theoretical Statistician Refined Federal Data-Collection Practices |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/44038436/william_kruskal_19192005/ |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |date=April 28, 2005 |pages=2–11 |via = [[Newspapers.com]] |accessdate=February 11, 2020}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref name=StAndrews>[http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Kruskal_William.html University of St Andrews, Scotland - School of Mathematics and Statistics: "William Kruskal" by J.J. O'Connor and E.F. Robertson] November 2006</ref>  His mother, [[Lillian Rose Vorhaus Kruskal Oppenheimer]], became a noted promoter of [[origami]] during the early era of television.<ref name="Obit"/>  He was the oldest of five children, three of whom, including himself, became researchers in mathematics and physics; see [[Joseph Kruskal]] and [[Martin Kruskal]].  Kruskal left [[Antioch College]] to attend [[Harvard University]], receiving bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics in 1940 and 1941.  He pursued a Ph.D. in [[mathematical sciences]] at [[Columbia University]], graduating in 1955 under the supervision of [[Henry Scheffé]] and [[Howard Levene]].<ref>{{cite web |title=William Kruskal - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=58995 |website=mathgenealogy.org |access-date=27 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250915152321/https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=58995 |archive-date=2025-09-15}}</ref> During the [[World War II|Second World War]], Kruskal served at the [[Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division|U.S. Naval Proving Ground]] in [[Dahlgren, Virginia]].  After brief stints working for his father and lecturing at Columbia, he joined the [[University of Chicago]] faculty as an instructor in statistics in 1950.

In 1958 he was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm View/Search Fellows of the ASA] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, accessed 2016-07-23.</ref>
He edited the [[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]] from 1958 to 1961, served as president of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] in 1971, and of the [[American Statistical Association]] in 1982.  Kruskal retired as professor emeritus in 1990.<ref name="Obit"/> In 1992 Kruskal was awarded the [[American Statistical Association Founders Award]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Founders Award | publisher=American Statistical Association | url=https://www.amstat.org/your-career/awards/founders-award }}</ref>

He died in [[Chicago]] in 2005.<ref name="Obit"/>
